topics.title: Tenali Raman-style wit: reading a clever tale

learn.hook: What wins in a king's court when there is no sword in your hand? A sharp mind and a quick, kind reply!
points: The lesson 'The Wit that Won Hearts' is about how clever, good-humoured thinking can win people over.
Tenali Raman (Tenali Ramakrishna) was a poet in the court of King Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire in the 16th century. Folk tales about his clever answers are told all over India.
Wit is the ability to think quickly and say something clever and amusing. A witty person solves a problem with words and ideas, not with force.
Most wit tales follow a pattern: a tricky challenge, a clever plan or reply, and a surprising ending that makes people laugh and learn.
Wit wins hearts when it is kind: it makes a point and makes people smile without hurting anyone.

example.q: Read: A proud merchant told the court, "I can sell anything, even air!" Tenali handed him an empty jar. "Then sell me this jar of fresh Vijayanagara breeze for one gold coin." The merchant peeped in and said, "But it is empty!" "Exactly," said Tenali, "and so was your boast." The whole court laughed, even the merchant. Think it through: what made Tenali's reply witty?
steps: The merchant made a big boast: he could sell anything, even air.
Tenali turned the boast into a test by offering a jar of 'air'.
When the merchant called the jar empty, Tenali said the boast was empty too.
The reply was quick and funny, and it made its point without being cruel, so even the merchant laughed.
example.answer: Tenali used the merchant's own words against him in a quick, funny way, showing that the boast had nothing behind it.

learn.reallife: When a friend teases you and you answer with a friendly comeback that makes everyone laugh, including your friend, that is wit in action.

games.title: Steps of a wit tale
games.prompt: Arrange the usual pattern of a clever-hero story
items: A challenge or problem appears
The clever hero thinks of a plan
The plan is carried out
A surprising twist reveals the trick
Everyone laughs and learns a lesson

games.title: Wit and the jar tale
items: Tenali Raman is linked with the court of King Krishnadevaraya.
Tenali Raman was a poet in Krishnadevaraya's court in the Vijayanagara Empire.
In the jar tale, the merchant managed to sell the air.
The merchant found the jar empty and could not sell anything.
Wit means thinking quickly and speaking cleverly.
That is the meaning of wit: quick, clever and amusing thinking.
The Vijayanagara Empire was in South India.
Its capital, Vijayanagara (Hampi), is in present-day Karnataka.
Birbal is the famous wit of King Krishnadevaraya's court.
Birbal is linked with Emperor Akbar's court. Tenali Raman is linked with Krishnadevaraya.
In the jar tale, the merchant laughed along with the court.
The tale says the whole court laughed, even the merchant.

quiz.q: Read: 'A proud merchant told the court, "I can sell anything, even air!"' Tenali later called this a boast. What does 'boast' mean?
quiz.explain: A boast is talking proudly about what you can do or have. The merchant proudly claimed he could sell anything.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'boast' with the similar-looking word 'boat'

quiz.q: Read: 'The merchant peeped in and said, "But it is empty!" "Exactly," said Tenali, "and so was your boast."' What does Tenali mean?
options: The merchant should buy a new jar
The jar was full of perfume
The merchant's claim had nothing real behind it
Tenali wanted the gold coin badly
quiz.explain: Tenali compares the empty jar to the empty boast: the merchant could not really sell 'anything'.
quiz.mistake: Takes the words literally and misses the comparison

quiz.q: Which phrase is closest in meaning to 'witty'?
quiz.explain: A witty person says clever things that also make people smile.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'witty' just means careful or quiet thinking

quiz.q: Tenali Raman's tales are set in the court of which king?
quiz.explain: Tenali Raman was a poet in the court of Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Tenali Raman with Birbal, who is linked with Akbar

quiz.q: Which of these is the best example of kind wit?
options: Making fun of a classmate's looks
A clever joke that makes everyone, even its target, laugh
Shouting louder than others in an argument
Copying someone's joke and claiming it as yours
quiz.explain: Kind wit makes a point and makes people laugh without hurting anyone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any joke at someone's cost counts as wit

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'foolish'?
quiz.explain: Foolish means lacking good sense; wise means having good sense. The other words are close to 'foolish', not opposite.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with a similar meaning instead of the opposite

quiz.q: In a wit tale, what usually happens right after the hero hears the challenge?
options: The hero thinks of a clever plan
quiz.explain: The pattern is challenge, then clever plan, then the twist and the laugh at the end.
quiz.mistake: Jumps to the ending and forgets the planning step

quiz.q: Read: The king sighed, "My cook burnt the rice again. What shall I do, Raman?" Raman bowed. "Make him eat it, Your Majesty. He will never burn it again!" Why is Raman's answer funny?
options: It is rude to the king
It is a very long speech
It is an unexpected but clever solution
quiz.explain: The answer is surprising, yet it makes sense: a cook who has to eat burnt rice will be careful next time.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that humour often comes from a surprising but sensible idea

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: What is 'wit'? How is a witty reply different from just being rude?
teach.praise: Chirp! Wit is quick, clever and funny, and it stays kind. Tenali would be proud of you!
teach.nudge: Is wit only about being clever? What should a witty reply do to the people listening, and should it hurt them?

learn.hook: If your friend says she is 'pulling your leg', should you check your leg? No! Welcome to the funny world of idioms.
points: Humour is the quality that makes something funny. 'Humour' is the British and Indian spelling; 'humor' is American. The adjective is 'humorous' in both, with no 'u' after the first 'o'.
Humour often comes from surprise, exaggeration (saying something is much bigger than it is) and funny misunderstandings.
An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words. 'Pulling my leg' means teasing me, not tugging my leg.

Useful humour idioms: crack a joke (tell a joke), in stitches (laughing a lot), keep a straight face (not laugh), tickled pink (very pleased), have the last laugh (win in the end after being doubted).

example.q: Think it through: Priya told Arjun, "Exams are cancelled forever!" Arjun's face lit up. Priya grinned, "I'm just pulling your leg!" What does Priya mean?
steps: Look at the idiom: 'pulling your leg'.
Nobody's leg is actually being pulled, so it is not literal.
Priya grinned after saying something too good to be true.
So the idiom means she was teasing or joking.
example.answer: Priya was joking; exams are not really cancelled.

learn.reallife: Comedy shows, cartoons and the jokes your grandparents tell at family dinners are full of exaggeration and idioms.

games.title: Idiom and meaning
pairs: win in the end after being doubted

items.text: The clown was so funny that the audience was in ___.
Dadaji tried to keep a ___ face while telling the joke.
Don't believe him, he is just pulling your ___.
Rohan loves to ___ jokes at the dinner table.
Everyone doubted the tortoise, but he had the last ___.

quiz.q: What does the idiom 'to pull someone's leg' mean?
quiz.explain: It is an idiom, so it is not about a real leg. It means joking with someone by telling them something untrue.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: 'The comedian had us in stitches.' This means the audience was ___.
quiz.explain: 'In stitches' means laughing so much that your sides hurt.
quiz.mistake: Thinks of stitches from sewing or a doctor

quiz.q: Which spelling of the noun meaning 'the quality of being funny' is used in British and Indian English?
quiz.explain: British and Indian English write 'humour'. 'Humor' is the American spelling.
quiz.mistake: Uses the American spelling

quiz.q: Which sentence uses exaggeration to be funny?
options: My school bag weighs a tonne!
I carried my bag to school.
quiz.explain: No school bag weighs a tonne (1000 kg). Saying so is a funny exaggeration, also called hyperbole.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the impossible amount

quiz.q: What is an idiom?
options: A word that sounds like another word
A word with the opposite meaning
A phrase whose meaning differs from its separate words
quiz.explain: In an idiom the words together have a special meaning, like 'in stitches' meaning laughing a lot.
quiz.mistake: Confuses idioms with homophones or antonyms

quiz.q: Meera kept a straight face while Ravi made funny faces. What did Meera do?
quiz.explain: To keep a straight face is to stop yourself from laughing.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'straight' literally

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'funny'?
quiz.explain: Amusing means causing laughter or a smile, which is what funny means. The others are nearly opposites.
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: Choose the correctly spelt adjective formed from 'humour'.
quiz.explain: Even in British English, the adjective drops the 'u': humorous.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the 'u' from 'humour' in the adjective

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: My friend said he was 'pulling my leg', but my leg is fine! What is an idiom?
teach.praise: Hee hee! An idiom is a phrase with a special meaning, so he was only teasing me. My leg is safe!
teach.nudge: Do the words in an idiom mean exactly what they say? And what was my friend really doing?

topics.title: Reported speech: telling what someone said

learn.hook: The king said something clever at dinner, and now the whole palace wants to know. How do you pass it on without quoting every word?
points: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: Tenali said, "I am ready."
Reported (indirect) speech gives the meaning without quotation marks, often with 'that': Tenali said that he was ready.
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, asked, told), the tense usually moves one step back: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, simple past → past perfect.
Pronouns and words of time and place change: I → he/she, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there, now → then, this → that.
Questions use 'asked' with if/whether (yes/no questions) or the wh-word, in normal statement order: The king asked where Tenali was going. Commands use told/ordered + to: The king told him to sit.

example.q: Change to reported speech: The king said, "I will reward the wisest man tomorrow."
steps: The reporting verb 'said' is in the past, so the tense moves back: will → would.
The pronoun changes: I → he (the king).
The time word changes: tomorrow → the next day.
Remove the quotation marks and add 'that'.
example.answer: The king said that he would reward the wisest man the next day.

learn.reallife: News reporters use reported speech all the time: 'The minister said that the bridge would open soon.' You use it too when you tell your parents what your teacher said.

games.title: Statement, question or command?
items: "I love mangoes."
"Where is my pen?"
"Close the door."
"Are you coming?"
"We won the match."
"Sit down quietly."
"Do not run in the corridor."
"Who broke the vase?"
"The tea is ready."

quiz.q: Choose the correct reported speech: Ria said, "I am hungry."
options: Ria said that she was hungry.
Ria said that I am hungry.
Ria said that she is being hungry.
Ria asked that she was hungry.
quiz.explain: 'I' becomes 'she' and 'am' moves back to 'was' after 'said'.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the pronoun or the tense

quiz.q: The king asked, "Where are you going, Tenali?" Choose the correct reported speech.
options: The king asked Tenali where was he going.
The king asked Tenali where he was going.
The king said Tenali where he was going.
The king asked Tenali that where he is going.
quiz.explain: In a reported question the word order becomes like a statement (he was going), and there is no question mark.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the question word order 'was he' in reported speech

quiz.q: Mother said to me, "Finish your homework." Choose the correct reported speech.
options: Mother said that I finish my homework.
Mother asked me if I finish my homework.
Mother told me finishing my homework.
Mother told me to finish my homework.
quiz.explain: A command is reported with 'told' + person + 'to' + verb.
quiz.mistake: Reports a command like a statement or a question

quiz.q: In reported speech after 'said', the word 'tomorrow' usually changes to ___.
quiz.explain: By the time the words are reported, 'tomorrow' is no longer tomorrow, so it becomes 'the next day'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the change for 'tomorrow' with the change for 'yesterday'

quiz.q: Arjun asked me, "Can you help me?" Choose the correct reported speech.
options: Arjun asked if I could help him.
Arjun asked can I help him.
Arjun asked if I can helped him.
Arjun said if I could help him.
quiz.explain: A yes/no question uses 'asked if'. 'Can' moves back to 'could', 'you' becomes 'I' and 'me' becomes 'him'.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the question form or uses 'said' for a question

quiz.q: Which sentence is in direct speech?
options: She said that she was tired.
They asked whether it was late.
quiz.explain: Direct speech gives the exact words inside quotation marks.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with 'said' is direct speech

quiz.q: Raju said, "I can solve this riddle." Complete: Raju said that he ___ solve that riddle.
quiz.explain: After a past reporting verb, 'can' moves back to 'could'.
quiz.mistake: Does not shift the modal back in reported speech

quiz.q: A yes/no question is reported using which word(s)?
quiz.explain: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' or 'whether': She asked if I was ready.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'that', which is for reported statements

teach.ask: Gappu flutters: My friend said, "I am going to the fair." How do I tell Mum what he said without using his exact words?
teach.praise: Tweet! 'He said that he was going to the fair.' Change the pronoun and step the tense back. Easy!
teach.nudge: What happens to the tense after 'said'? And does 'I' stay 'I' when you report someone else's words?
